prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Nothing says true love like releasing a caged butterfly, don't you think? Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin are to be paid $5 million for the picture rights to their wedding. The butterflies are reported to be the piece-de-resistance of England's most anticipated celebrity wedding of the year. Wayne Rooney, the best English footballer of his generation, and Coleen McLoughlin, his High School sweetheart, were to marry in an estimated $10 million ceremony in Italy Thursday. As they kiss, guests are apparently meant to open boxes and release the butterflies. The moment has been pilloried widely in the British media, tacky and over the top they all think, but is it just sour grapes? It has been a long and, at times, bumpy road for the couple to the altar. One littered with fierce criticism from the British press, which has enjoyed nothing more than lampooning Rooney and McLoughlin for being 'common.' The Daily Mail once even asked: "Is this Britain's ghastliest couple?" Rooney has been dubbed "Shrek" and "Mr Potato Head" due to his looks and his background as the son of a school dinner lady who grew up on a council estate is often referred to in a disparaging way. McLoughlin, meanwhile, has been subjected to page upon page of bitter stories about her weight, shopping sprees and her lack of closeness to Victoria Beckham. There has also been fierce criticism over the fact she has managed to become a millionaire in her own right. It's all down to Rooney apparently, and nothing to do with her appearing to be quite a decent person, who did well at school and has cleverly managed to parlay some of her fame into various media and advertising projects. Anyone who has seen her television show -- Coleen's Real Women -- can see she is a decent, bubbly person, who is very good at putting people at ease. Much to the media's fury, the couple have sold the rights to cover the wedding to OK magazine for a record $5 million. However they're not pocketing all the cash themselves, with an undisclosed sum from the fee to be donated to the Claire House children's hospice in Cheshire -- where McLoughlin's disabled foster sister Rosie is cared for. The queen's grandson, Peter Phillips and his bride Autumn Kelly, recently received $1m from Hello magazine to cover their wedding but they didn't receive an eighth of the opprobrium now directed at the more generous, but lower class, Rooney and McLoughlin. Moreover, in lieu of presents, Rooney and McLoughlin have also asked guests to donate money to the Alder Hey children's hospital in Liverpool. The wedding might be over the top, with a private yacht and luxury jet for guests (they are covering the guests' costs), expensive plonk and a $200,000 wedding dress, but at least the couple have worked hard for what they have. Their success despite a working-class background appears to be the greatest source of frustration for critics. It's just not on that someone who wasn't born into privilege and didn't go to a posh school can enjoy their wealth. That would be ugly. If anything, the couple's relationship and success is a triumph over adversity. They have known each other since McLoughlin was 12, but she spent two years fending off Rooney's entreaties to go out on a date. He finally got his chance when he saw her struggling to fix a broken bicycle chain. He rode over to help, popped the question again and got a yes. Surely they should be congratulated for creating their own modern fairytale complete with butterflies? The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

Rooney has been dubbed “Shrek” and “Mr. Potato Head” because of his appearance, while his background—as the son of a school dinner lady who grew up on a council estate—is often referenced disparagingly.

McLoughlin, meanwhile, has been subjected to page after page of bitter stories about her weight, shopping sprees and lack of closeness to Victoria Beckham. She has also faced fierce criticism for having managed to become a millionaire in her own right.

Apparently, it is all down to Rooney and has nothing to do with the fact that she appears to be a thoroughly decent person who did well at school and has cleverly parlayed some of her fame into various media and advertising projects.

Anyone who has seen her television show, “Coleen’s Real Women,” can see that she is a decent, bubbly person with a genuine talent for putting people at ease.

Much to the media’s fury, the couple have sold the rights to cover their wedding to OK! magazine for a record $5 million. However, they are not pocketing all the money themselves: an undisclosed portion of the fee will be donated to Claire House children’s hospice in Cheshire, where McLoughlin’s disabled foster sister, Rosie, is cared for.

The queen’s grandson, Peter Phillips, and his bride, Autumn Kelly, recently received $1 million from Hello! magazine for coverage of their wedding, yet they did not face even an eighth of the opprobrium now directed at the more generous—but lower-class—Rooney and McLoughlin.

He finally got his chance when he saw her struggling to repair a broken bicycle chain. He rode over to help, asked her out again—and this time received a yes.

Surely they should be congratulated for creating their own modern fairy tale, complete with butterflies?

The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

LONDON, England (CNN) — What could symbolize romance more dramatically than butterflies being freed from boxes?

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin will reportedly receive $5 million for exclusive photographs of their wedding. The butterfly release is expected to be the grand highlight of England’s most eagerly awaited celebrity marriage of the year.

Rooney, regarded as the finest English footballer of his generation, was due to marry McLoughlin, his school sweetheart, in Italy on Thursday. The ceremony is estimated to cost $10 million. According to reports, guests will open containers and set butterflies free when the couple kiss.

The British press has widely mocked the idea as excessive and tasteless. But could that reaction be driven by resentment?

The pair’s journey to marriage has been lengthy and sometimes difficult, marked by relentless attacks from newspapers that have delighted in ridiculing them as “common.” The Daily Mail once went so far as to ask, “Is this Britain’s ghastliest couple?”

Because of his appearance, Rooney has been called “Shrek” and “Mr Potato Head.” His upbringing is also frequently described in contemptuous terms: he is the son of a school dinner lady and was raised on a council estate.

McLoughlin has endured countless hostile articles about her weight, her expensive shopping trips and her supposedly distant relationship with Victoria Beckham. Critics have also objected strongly to the fact that she has become a millionaire independently.

Her achievements are often credited entirely to Rooney, with little recognition that she appears to be a genuinely pleasant person who performed well at school and has skillfully transformed her public profile into media and advertising opportunities. Viewers of her television program, *Coleen’s Real Women*, can see that she is cheerful, likable and particularly adept at making others feel comfortable.

To the press’s displeasure, the couple sold exclusive wedding coverage to *OK* magazine for a record $5 million. They will not, however, keep the entire payment. An unspecified portion will go to Claire House children’s hospice in Cheshire, where McLoughlin’s disabled foster sister, Rosie, receives care.

Peter Phillips, the Queen’s grandson, and his wife, Autumn Kelly, recently accepted $1 million from *Hello* magazine for coverage of their wedding. Yet they faced nowhere near one-eighth of the condemnation now aimed at Rooney and McLoughlin, who are both more generous and from a lower social class.

The couple have also asked guests to donate to Liverpool’s Alder Hey children’s hospital instead of buying wedding gifts.

Admittedly, the event may be extravagant. Plans reportedly include a private yacht, a luxury aircraft for guests—with Rooney and McLoughlin paying their expenses—costly alcohol and a wedding gown worth $200,000. Nevertheless, the pair have worked hard to earn their success.

What seems to trouble their critics most is that they prospered despite coming from working-class backgrounds. Apparently, people who were not born into privilege and did not attend elite schools are not supposed to enjoy their money. Now that would truly be unpleasant.

If anything, their romance and accomplishments represent a victory over hardship. They have known one another since McLoughlin was 12, although she rejected Rooney’s requests for a date for two years. His opportunity eventually arrived when he noticed her trying to repair a bicycle chain. He rode over, helped her, asked her out once more—and this time she agreed.

Surely a couple who have built their own contemporary fairytale, butterflies included, deserve congratulations.

The views stated in this commentary belong exclusively to the writer.

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s lavish Italian wedding offered the British press everything it expects from a major celebrity occasion: extravagant spending, carefully staged photographs, famous guests and conspicuous displays of romance. Among the most memorable details was the release of butterflies during the celebrations, a gesture that critics quickly portrayed as excessive and tasteless. The couple also reportedly secured a record magazine deal worth about $5 million, ensuring that exclusive access to the ceremony would become almost as significant as the wedding itself.

Yet the reaction to the event could not be separated from the way Rooney and McLoughlin had been treated throughout their years in the public eye. Both came from working-class Liverpool backgrounds, and much of the coverage focused less on their achievements than on their accents, clothes, appearance and spending habits. Rooney was routinely depicted as uncultured and awkward, while McLoughlin was mocked for her fashion choices, holidays and enthusiasm for designer goods. Even their attempts at sophistication were often presented as evidence that they did not truly belong in the wealthy world they had entered.

The wedding therefore became another opportunity for commentators to ridicule the couple’s taste. Details that might have been described as glamorous or romantic in the case of more socially approved celebrities were instead treated as vulgar. Their wealth was acknowledged, but their right to enjoy it was repeatedly questioned. Beneath the jokes lay a familiar form of British class prejudice: the assumption that people from modest backgrounds who acquire money through football or celebrity have no idea how to behave once they possess it.

This criticism also overlooked McLoughlin’s own success. She was frequently represented simply as a footballer’s fiancée, despite having built an independent public profile through media work, endorsements, fashion projects and magazine coverage. Her commercial appeal did not depend entirely on Rooney. She understood how celebrity culture operated and was able to convert intense public interest—much of it hostile—into professional opportunities and financial security.

The multimillion-dollar magazine agreement was a clear example of that instinct. Rather than allowing photographers and tabloids to profit freely from the event, the couple controlled access and sold the story on their own terms. The arrangement may have blurred the boundary between a private commitment and a commercial spectacle, but it also demonstrated a shrewd awareness of the value of their image. If the media was determined to follow, judge and photograph them, they were prepared to benefit from the attention.

None of this means the wedding was beyond criticism. Its scale and theatrical flourishes invited debate about excess, privacy and the commercialization of celebrity relationships. But the intensity and tone of the ridicule suggested something deeper than objections to extravagance. Rooney and McLoughlin seemed to provoke resentment because they were young, wealthy and unapologetically working-class—and because they refused to seek permission from traditional cultural gatekeepers before enjoying their success.

Seen in that light, the wedding was not merely a display of celebrity indulgence. It was also an illustration of the couple’s relationship with the British media: mocked for their background and taste, yet valuable enough to generate enormous sales. Rooney and McLoughlin learned to operate within that contradiction. The press could sneer at them, but the couple retained the power to turn its fascination into publicity, influence and profit.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style opinion commentary defending Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s lavish Italian wedding from accusations that it is tacky and excessive, emphasizing class prejudice in the British media.
counterfactuals.output:
### Opinion: The sneering at Wayne and Coleen’s wedding says more about Britain than it does about them

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s lavish Italian wedding has been greeted in predictable fashion: with fascination, followed by derision.

The cost, the clothes, the celebrity guests and the Mediterranean setting have all been offered as evidence that the occasion was not merely extravagant, but “tacky.” Yet that judgment reveals less about the couple’s taste than it does about Britain’s enduring discomfort with working-class people who acquire wealth—and then dare to enjoy it visibly.

There is nothing unusual about rich people staging spectacular weddings in Italy. Aristocrats, financiers and heirs have long treated Europe’s grandest hotels, villas and churches as private backdrops. Their celebrations are described as elegant, romantic or traditional. When a footballer and his childhood sweetheart do something similar, the vocabulary changes: suddenly it is vulgar, excessive and proof that money cannot buy class.

That double standard is class prejudice disguised as aesthetic criticism.

Rooney’s wealth did not come from inheritance or old social connections. It came from an extraordinary ability developed in a working-class community and tested in one of the world’s most competitive sports. McLoughlin, meanwhile, has been scrutinized for her clothes, accent and spending with an intensity rarely applied to women born into privilege. The message is difficult to miss: They may have earned access to luxury, but some commentators still believe they do not belong there.

Of course, nobody is obliged to admire an expensive wedding. At a time of economic hardship, displays of wealth can feel uncomfortable. But consistency matters. If extravagance itself is the objection, the same moral outrage should greet every society wedding, royal celebration and billionaire’s party. Too often, it does not.

Instead, working-class celebrity consumption is treated as uniquely offensive. The flowers become “gaudy.” The designer outfits become “showy.” The exclusive venue becomes “over the top.” Identical choices by the established elite are transformed into heritage and good taste.

Taste, in Britain, has never been merely personal. It has often functioned as a border patrol for class. Those already inside the gates are presumed to possess refinement; newcomers are expected to prove they deserve admission—and are mocked if they appear too delighted by what they have achieved.

Rooney and McLoughlin chose to celebrate their marriage on their own terms. They spent their own money, invited the people they loved and created an occasion that reflected their ambitions and personalities. It may not have been understated. It did not need to be.

The real vulgarity lies not in a lavish wedding, but in the spectacle of a media culture turning social snobbery into entertainment. Wayne and Coleen should not have to apologize for refusing to make their success small enough to comfort those who still confuse class with pedigree.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

### ROONEY WEDDING: FROM CROXTETH TO PORTOFINO

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin have completed their journey from childhood sweethearts to celebrity royalty with a lavish Italian wedding reportedly secured by a **$5 million magazine deal**.

The Manchester United star and his bride, both 22, exchanged vows during four days of celebrations around the Italian Riviera. Every extravagant detail seemed designed for the glossy pages: designer clothes, luxury yachts, famous footballing guests—and a romantic **butterfly release** after the ceremony, although the damp weather reportedly left some of the delicate participants reluctant to fly.

Yet amid the spectacle, Wayne and Coleen tried to keep one foot planted in their roots. The couple, who grew up in **working-class Croxteth, Liverpool**, met as teenagers long before Premier League wages, fashion contracts and paparazzi attention transformed their lives.

Guests were also encouraged to make **charitable donations rather than bring wedding presents**, with causes close to the couple benefiting from the celebration.

It was a wedding of striking contrasts: Liverpool childhood sweethearts surrounded by Mediterranean luxury, private jets and magazine exclusives. However grand the setting, the Rooneys’ strongest selling point remains the same—the idea that beneath all the celebrity trimmings, they are still Wayne and Coleen from Croxteth.

counterfactuals.prompt: Argue that the hostile press coverage of Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin reflects British snobbery rather than legitimate criticism of their extravagant wedding.
counterfactuals.output:
The hostile press coverage of Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s extravagant wedding can be seen less as a principled objection to excess than as an expression of British class prejudice. Wealthy aristocrats and established celebrities routinely stage lavish weddings, yet their spending is often described as elegant, romantic or traditional. When a footballer from a Liverpool council estate and his working-class fiancée did the same, the language shifted toward “tacky,” “vulgar” and “money cannot buy taste.” The objection was therefore not simply to extravagance, but to who was displaying it.

Rooney and McLoughlin disrupted an old social expectation that conspicuous luxury should belong to people with inherited wealth, polished accents and elite cultural credentials. Their celebration made newly acquired working-class wealth highly visible. Much of the ridicule focused on taste—clothes, decorations, celebrity guests and expensive gestures—because judgments about “taste” often function as coded judgments about class. The implication was that they could afford luxury but did not know how to perform it in the approved upper-middle-class manner.

The coverage also contained a gendered element. McLoughlin was frequently treated as a stereotypical footballer’s wife: acquisitive, shallow and famous only through her partner. Her appearance and consumer choices were scrutinised more harshly than the wealth and behaviour of male celebrities or aristocratic brides. Rooney’s regional background and public image likewise made him an easy target for commentators who equated refinement with southern, educated or upper-class manners.

There are legitimate grounds for criticising any spectacularly expensive wedding, especially amid economic inequality. But such criticism is credible only when applied consistently. If the press condemns working-class celebrities for extravagance while admiring similar excess among royalty, aristocrats or socially approved stars, it is not defending modesty; it is policing class boundaries. The intensity and vocabulary of the Rooney–McLoughlin coverage suggest that the real offence was not that they spent too much, but that they displayed wealth without possessing the social pedigree traditionally thought to legitimise it.

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s story has all the ingredients of a modern fairytale—if fairytales began on a council estate in Croxteth, unfolded beneath the glare of football fame, and featured paparazzi in place of wicked stepmothers.

The childhood sweethearts reportedly met at 12 and began dating at 16, long before Rooney became one of England’s biggest football stars. Their 2008 wedding on the Italian Riviera was the suitably extravagant royal-ball chapter: a multi-day celebration widely reported to have cost around £5 million, complete with luxury yachts, designer touches and a lucrative magazine deal.

Yet celebrity life brought more than sparkle. The tabloids chronicled their relationship with relentless enthusiasm, turning private difficulties, fashion choices and family dramas into front-page spectacle. Coleen was often reduced to a “WAG” caricature, while the couple’s troubles were treated as public property. Their endurance, however, has complicated the easy headlines: theirs is not a spotless story, but one repeatedly tested in full view of millions.

Away from the flashbulbs, both have also supported charitable causes, using their wealth and profile to raise funds for children, hospitals and disadvantaged communities. That philanthropy offers a quieter counterpoint to the tales of footballer excess and multimillion-pound celebrations.

Perhaps that is what makes the Rooney-McLoughlin romance feel distinctly modern. It is less “happily ever after” than “happily—and messily—ongoing”: two Liverpool teenagers who grew up together, became famous together and have tried to preserve a family life while the nation watched.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an opinion piece comparing media outrage over Coleen McLoughlin and Wayne Rooney selling their wedding photos to OK! magazine with the milder reaction to Peter Phillips and Autumn Kelly’s Hello! magazine deal.
counterfactuals.output:
## Two Weddings, Two Standards

When Coleen McLoughlin and Wayne Rooney sold the rights to their wedding photographs to *OK!* magazine, much of the press reacted as though the couple had committed an offence against matrimony itself. Their reported multimillion-pound deal was portrayed as vulgar, grasping and emblematic of celebrity culture at its worst. Every glossy detail seemed to confirm the prosecution’s case: here, apparently, was romance reduced to a commercial transaction.

Yet when Peter Phillips and Autumn Kelly agreed a lucrative deal with *Hello!* for coverage of their wedding, the indignation was noticeably more restrained. There was criticism, certainly—especially when members of the Royal Family, including the Queen, appeared in pictures published as part of the exclusive. But the overall tone was more embarrassed than enraged: an unfortunate lapse in judgement rather than proof of a fundamentally coarse character.

The contrast reveals less about the ethics of selling wedding photographs than about Britain’s enduring class prejudices.

Rooney, a footballer from Croxteth, and McLoughlin, whose fame grew alongside his, were already familiar targets. Their wealth did not buy them social legitimacy; if anything, it made them more suspect. Their spending could be described as “lavish”, their taste as “tacky” and their business decisions as evidence that they lacked the refinement expected of the truly privileged. They had money, but not the right kind of background.

Phillips, by contrast, is the Queen’s eldest grandchild. His deal could therefore be treated as a miscalculation by an otherwise respectable person. Royal connections provided a cushion unavailable to the Rooneys: one couple was accused of commodifying love, while the other was said merely to have mishandled the boundaries between private life and public status.

There are, of course, differences between the cases. Phillips was not a working royal and did not hold a title, while Rooney and McLoughlin were among the country’s most commercially valuable celebrities. But that distinction does not automatically make the *Hello!* deal less troubling. If anything, selling access to a wedding attended by the monarch raises more serious questions. A footballer owns his fame in a relatively straightforward sense: it derives from his profession and public appeal. Royal visibility, however, is bound up with inherited status and a national institution. Turning that access into private profit is not merely celebrity commerce; it risks trading on the Crown itself.

Nor is there anything inherently immoral about allowing a magazine to pay for wedding photographs. Famous people know that photographers will pursue them, newspapers will publish speculative stories and readers will consume the results. An exclusive can offer privacy, control and a way to offset the enormous cost of a highly scrutinised event. We may find the arrangement unromantic, but the modern media economy is hardly built on disinterested sentiment.

The real hypocrisy lies in pretending that commercialisation becomes vulgar only when practised by people with regional accents, football connections or conspicuous new wealth. The celebrity magazine market does not distinguish between aristocracy and show business; it turns both into content. The press, however, often does distinguish—harshly.

If selling a wedding is tasteless, then it is tasteless at St George’s Chapel as well as at an Italian palazzo. If it is simply a rational bargain between public figures and a hungry media, then the same defence should apply to both couples.

The unequal outrage suggests that Britain remains far more offended by social aspiration than by privilege. Rooney and McLoughlin were mocked for cashing in on fame they had earned. Phillips and Kelly received greater indulgence while cashing in, at least in part, on a status inherited by birth. That is not a moral distinction. It is a class judgement dressed up as one.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
